Abstract
The performance of visual SLAM systems, in terms of both robustness and accuracy, can be affected by the presence of 
dynamic objects in dynamic environments. The utilization of learning-based dynamic SLAM algorithms introduces addi-
tional challenges, such as increased power consumption and computing requirements, particularly on mobile platforms. 
Millimeter wave radar has the capability to directly detect and measure the relative velocity between objects and the radar 
system. Therefore, this paper presents a novel SLAM system that aims to integrate millimeter wave radar point clouds into 
visual SLAM in a dynamic environment. First, a real-time dynamic cluster extraction method was developed using Doppler 
information obtained from 4D radar. It effectively distinguishes between static background points and dynamic points by 
employing the RANSAC algorithm. The dynamic radar points are subsequently grouped together to create dynamic clusters. 
Then, the clusters are projected onto the image and expand to produce dynamic masks, taking into account the distribution 
characteristics. Finally, dynamic masks are employed to eliminate dynamic keypoints during the camera pose estimation, 
allowing for the estimation to be based solely on static keypoints. Experiments conducted in various daily dynamic scenarios 
have demonstrated the robustness of RDynaSLAM in operating effectively within dynamic environments. In comparison to 
ORBSLAM3, RDynaSLAM exhibits a notable reduction in the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of Absolute Pose Error 
(APE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE) in high dynamic environments. The method proposed in this paper has the capability 
to operate in real-time, without the need for GPU utilization.
Keywords  Visual SLAM · Dynamic environment · Motion segmentation · Real time · Robot
1  Introduction
The development of intelligent robots and autonomous 
assisted driving has led to the increasing importance of 
simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) technol-
ogy in the field of autonomous mobile robots and autono-
mous driving applications [1, 2]. The visual SLAM system 
employs low-cost cameras as primary sensors for locali-
zation and mapping. However, the existing visual SLAM 
systems, which are built on the assumption of a static 
environment, exhibit reduced accuracy and robustness when 
operating in dynamic environments [3].
In order to mitigate the influence of dynamic objects in 
the dynamic environment on the SLAM system, a commonly 
employed strategy involves detecting and excluding dynamic 
objects from the input images, thereby reducing their impact 
on pose estimation. Learning-based semantic models were 
employed [4–6] to detect dynamic objects against the static 
background. Moreover, some researchers incorporate geo-
metric constraints with semantic models into systems [7–9]. 
In most cases, the accuracy of these systems improved, but 
this came with a significant computational burden, espe-
cially for mobile platforms.
Meanwhile, data fusion from different sensors show 
greater robustness and less burden, eliminating the 
need to annotate data dependencies and deep models 
[10, 11]. Most of these methods detect ego-motion and 
detect dynamic object subsequently base on geometric 
constraints [12, 13]. On the other hand, dynamic objects

However, the resolution of the microphone array limits the 
detection of object sizes. With the ongoing improvement 
in the angular resolution of millimeter wave radar, it has 
acquired the ability to directly detect the size and velocity 
of reflected objects. Millimeter wave radar has the poten-

performance of SLAM systems in dynamic environments.
In this paper, we present RDynaSLAM, a novel SLAM 
system based on ORB-SLAM3, designed to operate effec-
tively in high dynamic environments, particularly, for 
social robot in dynamic indoor settings. The integration 
of a dynamic keypoints removal approach with the front 
end of RDynaSLAM including three models: dynamic 
objects clustering, dynamic mask generation, and robust 
pose estimation. A back-end, mainly including local map-
ping thread and a loop closing thread. The framework is 
illustrated in Fig. 1, which will be thoroughly explained in 
Section 3. RDynaSLAM operates in real-time within both 
highly dynamic and complex environments.
The main contributions of this paper as follows.
•	 A real-time dynamic cluster extraction methodology 
is proposed for acquiring dynamic clusters of dynamic 
objects using Doppler information from a 4D millimeter 
wave radar point cloud.
•	 A novel dynamic object mask generation pipeline is pro-
posed for data association, based on the distribution of 
expanded dynamic clusters.
•	 An approach for robust dynamic keypoints removal and 
pose estimation are proposed based on the dynamic 
object mask, considering the limited resolution of radar.
The remainder of this paper is arranged as follows. Sec-
tion 2 introduces the related work, Section 3 details the 
proposed method, and Section 4 focuses on the experiment 
results and analysis. Finally, Section 5 concludes.
2  Related Work
2.1  Dynamic Visual SLAM
The current strategy for improving visual SLAM in dynamic 
environments involves the removal of keypoints associated 
with dynamic objects from images. This process aims to 
decrease the number of dynamic points in the map and miti-
gating the impact of dynamic objects on the accuracy of 
localization.
Based on the assumption that the subject in the image is 
stationary, Sun et al. [15] employed the RANSAC algorithm 
to compute the homography matrix between two consecu-
tive frames. It is not appropriate for high dynamic scenes in 
which dynamic keypoints dominate the main composition 
of the image. Wei et al. [16] proposed the GMSK-SLAM 
system combines the Grid based Motion Statistics (GMS) 
feature matching with the K-means clustering to effectively 
detect dynamic regions. Dai et al. [17] utilized the Delaunay 
triangulation [18] to connect the relatively static keypoints 
in sequential image. However, the assumption that largest 
region represents a static background, makes this system 
unsuitable for high dynamic scenarios.
The method that combines prior semantic information 
does not preset the proportion of dynamic features. Semantic 
annotation model (YOLO [19], SegNet [20], Mask R-CNN 
[21]) is designed to annotate semantics and incorporates 
prior knowledge to remove dynamic objects. The model’s 
ability to perform semantic annotation relies on the avail-
ability of training data, with significant computational 
burden and low efficiency. The DynaSLAM system, pro-
posed by Bescos et al. [4], utilizes Mask R-CNN to seg-
ment and remove moving objects. Fan et al. [22] designed 
BlitzSLAM for indoor dynamic environments based on 
ORBSLAM2, with Blitz networks and polar constraints. To 
alleviate the computational burden of semantic extraction 
models, Wu et al. [23] introduced a dynamic feature selec-
tion approach in the YOLO-SLAM system. This method 
integrates object detection, depth difference, and RANSAC 
to approximate semantic segmentation for efficiency. Liu 
et al. [24] introduced a semantic segmentation thread and a 
semantic optimization thread into the RDS-SLAM system 
based on ORB-SLAM3 [25]. A strategy, developed for the 
response of semantic requests, operates nearly 15 frames/s 
with RTX2080ti. RDMOSLAM [26] incorporates additional 
threads for optical flow and speed estimation threads in con-
junction with RDS-SLAM. The system utilizes optical flow

The use of sensors such as LiDAR and IMU in SLAM 
tasks has led to increased focus on the multi-sensor comple-

information or environmental presets, but it also imposes 
greater demands on system installation accuracy and fusion 
algorithms [27]. Fu et al. [28–30] transformed the current

utilizing IMU data. Subsequently, they filtered dynamic 
keypoints based on the consistency between motions of 
keypoints and camera. A wheeled odometer, similar to an 
IMU, can provide motion constraints for the camera. The 
DRE-SLAM proposed by Yang et al. [13] utilizes a wheeled 
odometer to obtain the pose transformation matrix of adja-

based on motion consistency. Zhang et al. [14] used a micro-
phone array to determine the direction of a moving object, 
deleted the corresponding image features in the frame, 
and established a map by utilizing the residual stationary 
keypoints.
2.2  Radar‑Visual Fusion
The camera possesses a high angular resolution and has the 
capability to capture precise object shapes, but it faces chal-
lenges in determining the spatial position and velocity of 
objects. The millimeter wave radar possesses a high range 
resolution, enabling direct detection of the speed and dis-
tance of objects. Nevertheless, the radar’s ability to accu-
rately identify the shape of the objects is hindered by its low 
resolution in pitch and azimuth. The combination of radar 
and camera has demonstrated outstanding performance in 
various tasks, including object detection and tracking, as 
well as scene flow estimation.
In object detection, the ROI of the target in the image is 
usually initially generated from radar data. Subsequently, 
object recognition is performed within the ROI area. The 
utilization of ROI-based methods can significantly reduce 
computational complexity. However, the presence of radar 
multipath effects results in the occurrence of false ROIs 
and overlapping ROIs within the image. On the other hand, 
deep learning has demonstrated impressive performance and 
robustness in end-to-end radar vision fusion object detection 
frameworks [31–33].
In the field of object tracking, fusion strategies are cat-
egorized into early fusion and late fusion. The early fusion 
approach involves initially matching radar data with images, 
followed by tracking the objects. Late fusion involves the 
separate tracking of objects using radar and camera, fol-
lowed by their combination. Reference [34] used radar to 
provide ROI for object detection in images, and then merged 
the image with the target trajectory in the radar based on 
Euclidean distance.
In the field of scene flow estimation, traditional scene 
flows are obtained from RGB or RGB-D images using prior 
knowledge or supervised and unsupervised deep networks. 
With the application of learning-based feature extraction in 
point cloud [35–37], these methods has led to the dominance 
of point cloud-based scene flow estimation [38] and [39]. 
The self-supervised method for radar scene flow estima-
tion was proposed by Reference [40], while the absence of 
ground truth constrains their performance. Reference [41] 
proposes a 4D radar scene flow estimation method based on 
cross modal learning with the guidance from different sen-
sors (including LiDAR, camera, and GPS/INS).
2.3  Differences from Related Works
In contrast to the prevailing dynamic SLAM systems, which 
rely on prior knowledge and deep semantic models or are 
based on the assumption of stationary image subjects. Our 
research primarily centers on developing a SLAM system 
that is not reliant on prior information, is lightweight, and 
can operate effectively in a high dynamic environment.
The SLAM system most closely to RDynaSLAM is the 
one described in reference [14]. To our knowledge, this rep-
resents the first dynamic SLAM system designed based on 
sound source localization. However, this system is unable to 
identify quiet dynamic objects and static objects with noise. 
As a result, numerous static points are incorrectly removed 
along with dynamic points, and the remaining points are 
insufficient for tracking in highly dynamic environments. 
The RDynaSLAM system employs 4D millimeter wave 
radar for direct measurement of the relative velocity of 
objects in the surrounding environment. In particular, utiliz-
ing the high-resolution 4D millimeter wave radar, a method 
for detecting the shapes and locations of dynamic objects. In 
response to the problem of misjudgment of dynamic points 
on the boundary, a two-step verification method for dynamic 
points was developed to accurately remove them during the 
positioning and mapping process.
3  Approach
3.1  Overview
ORB-SALM3 is a sparse visual SLAM system that has 
achieved good performance in static environments, while 
lacks robustness and accuracy in dynamic environments. 
This article focuses on the specific needs for localization 
and mapping of robots within dynamic indoor environ-
ments. It also explores the potential of millimeter wave

images. Using 4D millimeter wave radar to directly detect 
dynamic objects, and then label dynamic regions in the 
image, the RDynaSLAM system is proposed based on the 
ORB-SLAM3.
The overview of the proposed RDynaSLAM system is 
show in Fig. 2. In this system, the 4D radar point clouds 
are firstly fed into the RANSAC algorithm to fit the static 
background using doppler data. Secondly, the moving 4D 
point are extracted by the distance between the point and the 
static background plane. Since the extracted moving points 
are contaminated with noise points, the DBSCAN cluster-
ing algorithm is employed to eliminate the noise points and 
establish moving clusters. Thirdly, the clusters are projected 
onto image by conversion matrix of the camera and radar. 
The dynamic mask is formed by the distribution and posi-
tion of points in the clusters. The static keypoints that fall 
within the mask will be selected based on the reprojection 
error, since the inherent imperfections of the dynamic mask 
obtained through radar. The camera pose is determined by 
all static keypoints at last.
3.2  Real‑Time Dynamic Cluster Extraction in 4D 
Point Cloud
Due to the high resolution of 4D radar, dynamic objects 
exhibit multiple reflection points in the radar point cloud. 
The presence of reflection and interference, the point cloud 
not only contains static and dynamic objects, but also sig-
nificant amount of noise points. Therefore, the extraction of 
moving points from point clouds involves the filtration of 
static background and extraneous noise points. This article 
assumes that the subject of the point cloud remains station-
ary and employs velocity information from the point cloud 
to design a real-time dynamic clustering algorithm. Algo-
rithm 1 outlines the procedure, while Fig. 3 illustrates the 
steps involved in acquiring dynamic point clouds, dynamic 
clusters, and projecting these points onto the image.

4.1  Evaluation of Dynamic Keypoints Removal
The quantity of dynamic keypoints plays a crucial role in 
determining the precision and resilience of a SLAM system 
in dynamic environments. To assess the system’s ability to 
eliminate dynamic features, both static and dynamic key-
points are tallied from frames captured at 3-second inter-
vals. Typically, in scenarios with low dynamics, dynamic 
keypoints account for less than 50%, whereas in highly 
dynamic environments, they constitute over 50% of the total 
keypoints.
As shown in Table 1, the proportions of dynamic key-
points is observed to be close and far from 50% in low 
dynamic scenes, such as single_corridor1, suggesting a min-
imal impact on both systems. In both systems, the RANSAC 
algorithm is employed for outlier removal in pose estima-
tion and performs effectively when outliers are fewer than 
50%. In high dynamic scenes, such as single_corridor3 and 
two_corridor1, a majority of dynamic keypoints are fil-
tered out by the 4D radar, although not entirely eliminated. 
The utilization of dynamic keypoints in our system is sig-
nificantly below 50%, whereas in ORB-SLAM3, it exceeds 
50%, indicating a notable enhancement of RdynaSLAM in 
highly dynamic environments.

4.3  Analysis of the Efficiency
In practical applications, real-time performance is a critical 
metric for evaluating SLAM systems. Due to the substantial 
computing resources required for map construction, we con-
struction map on a computer equipped with 8GB of RAM 
and an E3–1270 V2 processor in offline mode.
For each frame, as shown in Table 4, the time consump-
tion of our pose estimation module has an average increase 
of only 1.15 ms compared to ORB-SLAM3, thus satisfying 
real-time requirements.
5  Conclusions and Discussion
This paper introduces RDynaSLAM, a real-time SLAM 
system designed to operate effectively in highly dynamic 
environments. The primary concept behind RDynaSLAM 
involves leveraging Doppler information acquired from radar 
to assist the visual SLAM system in mitigating interference 
caused by moving objects. Using the doppler information, 
the system generates dynamic object masks based on the dis-
tribution of radar points, and subsequently divides the image 
into static areas and potential dynamic areas. The keypoints 
in the static area are utilized for the initial pose estimation, 
after which any outliers in the potential dynamic area are 
eliminated by the reprojection error. Experiment shows 
that RDynaSLAM is capable of real-time pose estimation 
in a dynamic environment. Simultaneously, the system has 
the capability to adjust to alterations in the motion state 
of objects and efficiently eliminate the impact of dynamic 
objects. However, there are some works need to be furthered.
Firstly, RDynaSLAM depends on millimeter wave radar for 
perceiving dynamic objects in the surrounding environment. 
The reflection characteristics of millimeter-waves result in the 
appearance of mirror images of dynamic objects in the point 
cloud. The presence of walls, guardrails, and other flats can 
result in multiple moving objects present in the point cloud, even 
when only a single object is in motion. This could potentially 
lead to the removal of static keypoints, consequently impacting 
the accuracy of pose estimation. In addressing this problem, the 
fusion of visual and millimeter-wave point clouds can be utilized 
to detect planes, thereby identifying mirror targets.
Secondly, the map will unavoidably incorporate certain 
dynamic object points as a result of issues like the failure of 
dynamic object detection or alterations in the motion state 
of dynamic objects. These dynamic map points will impact 
on the accuracy of pose estimation. Current research often 
overlooks the dynamic objects already present in the map. 
While the approach outlined in this article could mitigate 
the influence of dynamic objects in the map, it does not have 
the capability to remove dynamic objects from the map. To 
address this problem, a specific mechanism could be imple-
mented to continuously validate the existence of map points 
to uphold a certain frequency of map updates.

Abstract: The performance of visual SLAM systems, in terms of both robustness and accuracy, can be affected by the presence of dynamic objects in dynamic environments. The utilization of learning-based dynamic SLAM algorithms introduces addi- tional challenges, such as increased power consumption and computing requirements, particularly on mobile platforms. Millimeter wave radar has the capability to directly detect and measure the relative velocity between objects and the radar system. Therefore, this paper presents a novel SLAM system that aims to integrate millimeter wave radar point clouds into visual SLAM in a dynamic environment. First, a real-time dynamic cluster extraction method was developed using Doppler information obtained from 4D radar. It effectively distinguishes between static background points and dynamic points by employing the RANSAC algorithm. The dynamic radar points are subsequently grouped together to create dynamic clusters. Then, the clusters are projected onto the image and expand to produce dynamic masks, taking into account the distribution characteristics. Finally, dynamic masks are employed to eliminate dynamic keypoints during the camera pose estimation, allowing for the estimation to be based solely on static keypoints. Experiments conducted in various daily dynamic scenarios have demonstrated the robustness of RDynaSLAM in operating effectively within dynamic environments. In comparison to ORBSLAM3, RDynaSLAM exhibits a notable reduction in the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of Absolute Pose Error (APE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE) in high dynamic environments. The method proposed in this paper has the capability to operate in real-time, without the need for GPU utilization.
